title: Enzyme
body: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, facilitating chemical reactions in cells by lowering the activation energy.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 — "Enzymes are proteins that are biological catalysts that facilitate chemical reactions in cells by lowering the activation energy"

title: Enzyme-substrate complex model
body: A reaction occurs only when the shape and charge of the substrate are compatible with the active site of the enzyme.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2 — "the shape and charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site of the enzyme"

title: Denaturation
body: Disruption of a protein's structure by a change in temperature, pH, or chemical environment, which eliminates its ability to catalyze reactions.
caution: In some cases denaturation is reversible, so the enzyme can regain activity (3.2.A.2).
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.i — "Denaturation of proteins, such as enzymes, occurs when the protein structure is disrupted"

title: Temperature and pH outside the optimum range
body: Temperature or pH outside an enzyme's optimal range changes its structure by disrupting hydrogen bonds, which alters the efficiency with which it catalyzes reactions.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.ii — "outside the optimal range for a given enzyme will cause changes to its structure (by disrupting the hydrogen bonds)"

title: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
body: Higher temperature increases molecular speed and the frequency of enzyme-substrate collisions, so reaction rate increases until the optimal temperature is reached.
ced_evidence: 3.2.B.2 — "increasing the rate of reaction until the optimal temperature is achieved"

title: Substrate and product concentration
body: The relative concentrations of substrates and products determine how efficiently an enzymatic reaction proceeds.
ced_evidence: 3.2.B.1 — "The relative concentrations of substrates and products determine how efficiently an enzymatic reaction proceeds"

title: Competitive inhibitor
body: A molecule that binds reversibly to the active site of the enzyme.
ced_evidence: 3.2.B.3 — "Competitive inhibitor molecules can bind reversibly to the active site of the enzyme"

title: Noncompetitive inhibitor
body: A molecule that can bind to an allosteric site, changing the activity of the enzyme.
ced_evidence: 3.2.B.3 — "Noncompetitive inhibitors can bind to allosteric sites, changing the activity of the enzyme"

title: Life, order, and the laws of thermodynamics
body: Life requires a highly ordered system and does not violate the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

items.label: i
items.meaning: Energy input must exceed energy loss to maintain order and to power cellular processes.

items.label: ii
items.meaning: Cellular processes that release energy may be coupled with cellular processes that require energy.

items.label: iii
items.meaning: Significant loss of order or energy flow results in death.

ced_evidence: 3.3.A.2 — "Life requires a highly ordered system and does not violate the first and second laws of thermodynamics"

title: Metabolic pathway (sequential energy pathway)
body: Energy-related pathways are sequential to allow more controlled energy transfer, and a product of one reaction is typically the reactant for the next step.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.3 — "A product of a reaction in a metabolic pathway is typically the reactant for the subsequent step in the pathway"

title: Domains sharing conserved core metabolic pathways
body: Core metabolic pathways such as glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation are conserved across all currently recognized domains, which supports common ancestry.

items.label: Archaea
items.meaning: Domain with conserved core metabolic pathways

items.label: Bacteria
items.meaning: Domain with conserved core metabolic pathways

items.label: Eukarya
items.meaning: Domain with conserved core metabolic pathways

ced_evidence: 3.3.B.1 — "conserved across all currently recognized domains (Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya)"

title: Photosynthesis
body: The series of reactions that use carbon dioxide, water, and light energy to make carbohydrates and oxygen.
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.1 — "series of reactions that use carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), and light energy to make carbohydrates and oxygen (O2)"

title: Evolution of photosynthesis
body: Evidence-based statements about the origin of photosynthesis and its effects.

items.label: First evolved
items.meaning: Photosynthesis first evolved in prokaryotic organisms.

items.label: Oxygenated atmosphere
items.meaning: Scientific evidence supports that prokaryotic (cyanobacterial) photosynthesis produced an oxygenated atmosphere.

items.label: Eukaryotic photosynthesis
items.meaning: Prokaryotic photosynthetic pathways were the foundation of eukaryotic photosynthesis.

ced_evidence: 3.4.A.1.ii–iv — "Photosynthesis first evolved in prokaryotic organisms"

title: Chloroplast structure and where photosynthetic reactions occur
body: Labelled regions of the chloroplast and the reactions located in each.

items.label: Stroma
items.meaning: Fluid within the inner chloroplast membrane and outside the thylakoid; site of carbon fixation (Calvin cycle) reactions

items.label: Thylakoid membranes
items.meaning: Contain chlorophyll pigments organized into two photosystems, plus electron transport proteins

items.label: Grana
items.meaning: Stacks of thylakoids; site of the light reactions

ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 — "Stroma and thylakoids are found within the chloroplast"

title: Light reactions to Calvin cycle: energy flow
body: Energy captured from light is transferred to ATP and NADPH, which power carbohydrate production in the Calvin cycle.

items.label: Light reactions (grana)
items.meaning: Capture energy present in light to yield ATP and NADPH

items.label: ATP and NADPH
items.meaning: Carry the captured energy

items.label: Calvin cycle (stroma)
items.meaning: Uses ATP and NADPH to produce carbohydrates from carbon dioxide

ced_evidence: 3.4.B.6 — "powers the production of carbohydrates from carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle. This occurs in the stroma"

title: Electron transport chain (ETC)
body: A series of oxidation-reduction reactions that transfer electrons between molecules and establish an electrochemical proton gradient across a membrane.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.4 / 3.5.A.3 — "transfers electrons in a series of oxidation-reduction reactions that establish an electrochemical gradient across membranes"

title: Light reactions: electron and proton flow
body: Order of events in the light reactions of photosynthesis in the thylakoid membrane.

items.meaning: Chlorophylls absorb light energy, boosting electrons to a higher energy level in photosystems I and II
Water splits, supplying electrons to replace those lost from photosystem II
Electrons pass through the ETC connecting photosystems II and I in oxidation/reduction reactions
A proton gradient forms across the thylakoid membrane (high inside, low outside)
Electrons are ultimately transferred to NADP+, reducing it to NADPH in photosystem I
Protons flow back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), forming ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate (photophosphorylation)

ced_evidence: 3.4.B.2–3.4.B.5 — "Water then splits, supplying electrons to replace those lost from photosystem II"

title: Proton gradient direction in the thylakoid
body: Protons are at high concentration inside the thylakoid membrane and low concentration outside it.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.4 — "a region of low proton concentration outside the thylakoid membrane from a region of high proton concentration inside"

title: Chemiosmosis
body: The flow of protons back through membrane-bound ATP synthase, which drives the formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.5 / 3.5.A.3.iii — "The flow of protons back through membrane-bound ATP synthase by chemiosmosis drives the formation of ATP"

title: Photophosphorylation
body: The formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate driven by chemiosmosis through ATP synthase in photosynthesis.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.5 — "this is known as photophosphorylation"

title: Oxidative phosphorylation
body: The formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate driven by chemiosmosis through ATP synthase in aerobic cellular respiration.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3.iii — "This is known as oxidative phosphorylation in aerobic cellular respiration"

title: Glycolysis
body: A biochemical pathway that releases the energy in glucose molecules to form ATP, NADH, and pyruvate.
ced_evidence: 3.5.B.1 — "releases the energy in glucose molecules to form ATP (from ADP and inorganic phosphate), NADH (from NAD+), and pyruvate"

title: Krebs (citric acid) cycle
body: Takes place in the mitochondrial matrix; releases CO2 from organic intermediates, synthesizes ATP, and transfers electrons to the coenzymes NAD+ and FAD, forming NADH and FADH2.
ced_evidence: 3.5.B.2–3.5.B.3 — "The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix"

title: Fermentation
body: A process that allows glycolysis to proceed in the absence of oxygen and produces organic molecules such as alcohol and lactic acid.
ced_evidence: 3.5.B.6 — "Fermentation allows glycolysis to proceed in the absence of oxygen"

title: Aerobic cellular respiration in eukaryotes: order of stages
body: Sequence of stages by which energy from glucose is used to make ATP.

items.label: Glycolysis (cytosol)
items.meaning: Glucose is converted to ATP, NADH, and pyruvate

items.label: Pyruvate transport
items.meaning: Pyruvate moves from the cytosol to the mitochondrion, where oxidation occurs

items.label: Krebs cycle (matrix)
items.meaning: Releases CO2; reduces NAD+ to NADH and FAD to FADH2; synthesizes ATP

items.label: ETC (inner mitochondrial membrane)
items.meaning: NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons; the terminal electron acceptor is oxygen; a proton gradient forms

items.label: Chemiosmosis
items.meaning: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, forming ATP (oxidative phosphorylation)

ced_evidence: 3.5.B.2–3.5.B.4 — "Electrons extracted in glycolysis and Krebs cycle reactions are transferred by NADH and FADH2 to the ETC"

title: Proton gradient direction in the mitochondrion
body: Protons are at high concentration outside the inner membrane (intermembrane space) and low concentration inside (matrix), so the matrix pH is higher than the intermembrane space.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3.ii / 3.5.B.5 — "The pH inside the mitochondrial matrix is higher than in the intermembrane space"

title: Terminal electron acceptor
body: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration; aerobic prokaryotes use oxygen, while anaerobic prokaryotes use other molecules.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3.i — "toward the terminal electron acceptor, oxygen"

title: Mitochondrion: regions and functions in respiration
body: Labelled mitochondrial parts and the processes associated with each.

items.label: Matrix
items.meaning: Site of the Krebs cycle; lower proton concentration and higher pH

items.label: Inner mitochondrial membrane
items.meaning: Contains the ETC and ATP synthase; folding increases surface area so more ATP can be synthesized

items.label: Intermembrane space / outside the inner membrane
items.meaning: Region of high proton concentration

ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3.ii — "The folding of the inner membrane increases the surface area, which allows for more ATP to be synthesized"

title: Decoupling oxidative phosphorylation generates heat
body: In aerobic respiration, decoupling oxidative phosphorylation from electron transport generates heat, which endothermic organisms can use to regulate body temperature.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3.iv — "decoupling oxidative phosphorylation from electron transport generates heat"

title: Required components of a constructed graph
body: Components a graph must include (CED skill 4.A).

items.label: i
items.meaning: Type of graph appropriate for the data

items.label: ii
items.meaning: Axis labeling, including appropriate units and legend

items.label: iii
items.meaning: Scaling

items.label: iv
items.meaning: Accurately plotted data (including error bars when appropriate)

items.label: v
items.meaning: Trend line (when appropriate)

ced_evidence: Skill 4.A — "Construct a graph to represent the data"
